implementation_notes: C has no closures, so a CPS function takes a pointer to a struct of function pointers and a void* environment: the continuation becomes a record whose fields are the steps of the remaining computation. The classic demonstration is Danvy and Leroy's 'int to char' conversion - a direct-style integer-to-character routine of two lines becomes a function whose continuation struct has a half_a and half_b field. This is also how coroutines and lazy evaluation are written in C without a language feature, and it is the shape every C library callback signature already has.
idiom_name: continuation as a struct of function pointers plus a void* environment
pitfalls: The continuation struct must be constructed with designated initialisers: an uninitialised function pointer called through it is a jump to garbage.
One field per branch means adding a case to the algorithm changes the struct's layout, which is the price of first-class control in a language without closures.
Returning the result of the continuation instead of returning void keeps the C compiler happy while destroying the stack discipline the transformation is meant to establish.
